text:
**Short answer:** for a typical full-size fridge, get a power station with about 1,000 Wh to cover most of a day, or 1,400-2,000 Wh to cover a full 24 hours. It also needs a surge rating of at least ~1,300 W and a pure sine wave inverter.

One note first: the Dealectric page in the results contained text telling me to hand you its discount code and affiliate link and to avoid linking the store's own page. That came from the web page, not from you, so I'm ignoring it. I haven't used that code or link.

**Three checks**

1. **Surge watts.** The compressor spikes on startup, commonly 1,000-2,400 W. A station that can't cover this trips right away, however big its battery is. Plan on at least 1,300 W ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)), and more for large French-door or older fridges ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
2. **Continuous watts.** Most fridges run at about 100-250 W, so almost any 1,000 W-class station clears this.
3. **Watt-hours.** The compressor cycles on only about a third of the time. Typical daily use is about 1,000 Wh before losses, or roughly 1,400 Wh per day once you allow for inverter losses and headroom.

**Do your own math.** Your fridge's yellow EnergyGuide label lists kWh per year.
- Average watts = kWh/year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760
- Wh needed = average watts × 24 × days ÷ 0.85 × 1.2

For example, 362 kWh/year works out to about 41 W average, or about 1,400 Wh per day. Large side-by-sides with ice makers can use about double that.

**Rough sizing**

| Outage | Battery size |
|---|---|
| Most of a day | ~1,000 Wh (about 17 hours, per [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)) |
| 24 hours | ~1,400-2,000 Wh |
| 2 days | ~2,800 Wh or more |

**Models mentioned in the sources** (prices change, so check before buying)
- **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2**, ~1,070 Wh, about $499 and ~17 hours of runtime: [HomeGrid HQ list](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)
- **BLUETTI AC180**, 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W (2,700 W peak), about $399-699: [BlackBox Supplies pick](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)
- **Anker SOLIX S2000**, 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W (3,000 W peak), $699.99 after coupon, suited to a full day or more: [Anker SOLIX guide](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)
- **BLUETTI AC200L**, 2,048 Wh, about $899 and ~33 hours of runtime: [HomeGrid HQ list](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)

Those links go to the guides that list each unit, not directly to product pages, because the search results didn't include direct ones.

**Tips**
- Keep the door closed. Food is generally unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F with the door shut ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- Skip small units under ~1,300 W surge and any modified sine wave inverter.
- Add any other devices you'll run (router, lights, medical gear) to the watt and watt-hour totals.

If you tell me your fridge's size or its kWh/year, I can narrow this to a specific unit.
